poiANC-desc:
The Andean Compact is the one great power of South America that came out of the Dark Age richer than it went in. Its heartland is the old Andes: Peru, the highland republics of Surandes, and the Distrito del Litio, whose salt flats and mining districts supply the lithium that keeps batteries charged on four continents. Its capital, Lima, looks out over a Pacific that the Great Mistake treated more gently than most.

The Compact is a confederation more than a state. Power is shared between a modest central government, the corporations and cooperatives that run the mines, and the indigenous groups that hold the land beneath them. Politics is a crowded field, but none of the movements is strong enough to rule alone. Few citizens seem to mind. Wages are decent, the schools are full, and the lights stay on.

Abroad, the Compact is both patron and villain. Lima shelters the elected government of Brazil in exile and pays for its survival, which the Compact calls solidarity. Brasilia calls it conquest, and blames the Andes for every shortage in its cities. Compact officials answer that lithium is sold and not stolen, and that nobody has ever been forced to buy it.

Wealth has made the Compact confident, and confidence has made it careless. A country that depends on one resource, and on companies that answer to no one, can only stay a power for as long as the mines and the contracts hold.
ANCpoi001-desc: The century turns yet again, but the Andes stand tall. The world is crumbling under the pressure of ancient struggles and climate change, but the Andean Compact is stronger than ever. Bolstered by international investors, vast energy reserves, a literate population and good geography, the Compact is widely recognized as a world power. The citizens of the Compact enjoy many social, economic, and technological freedoms that are rare in other parts of the world. The Compact is in its golden age, and it's going to last.
ANCpoi002-desc: Old Peru and Bolivia are home to some of the world's largest lithium reserves. Monopolized by local indigenous groups, the lithium trade is one of the pillars on which the entire Compact rests. While international trade isn't quite as extensive as in pre-Mistake times, the export of lithium has made the Andes rich and powerful.
ANCpoi003-desc:
Major corporations and interest groups control the Compact's economy. The government has little say on where to build, what to build, and when to build it. Any legislation is instantly met with a flurry of pushbacks and filibustering, while the parties are too busy fighting one another to form a united front.

The military is no more centralized. The government has limited control over a patchwork of militias, mercenaries, and a few official divisions whose loyalty is more than a little questionable. On the plus side, companies fund and equip their own forces out of pocket.
